```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
tutorial_options(exercise.timelimit = 60)
```

## PCA is SVD, applied to centered data

In Tutorial 1 you built a centered genotype matrix `Gc` and formed
`t(Gc) %*% Gc`, a samples-by-samples similarity matrix. In Tutorial 2 you
saw that any matrix decomposes as $A = U D V^\top$: rotate, stretch,
rotate.

Principal Components Analysis is nothing more than: **center your data,
then take its SVD.** The "principal components" are new coordinates --
linear combinations of the original variables -- chosen so that the first
one captures as much spread (variance) in the data as a single direction
possibly can, the second captures as much of what's left as a direction
orthogonal to the first can, and so on.

## A 2-variable toy example

Before genotypes, use two correlated variables you can plot directly.

```{r toy-data, exercise=TRUE}
set.seed(42)
n <- 60
x <- rnorm(n, sd = 2)
y <- 0.8 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 0.7)
toy <- cbind(x, y)
plot(toy, asp = 1, pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
     main = "Two correlated variables")
```

Just by looking at the scatterplot: is there a direction along which these
points are most spread out? Is there a roughly perpendicular direction
along which they are much less spread out?

```{r quiz-look, echo=FALSE}
quiz(
  question("Looking at the scatterplot, along which direction are the points most spread out?",
    answer("Roughly along the diagonal, where x and y increase together", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Exactly along the x-axis"),
    answer("Exactly along the y-axis"),
    answer("There is no direction of greater spread; it's spread evenly in all directions"),
    allow_retry = TRUE
  )
)
```

## Centering, then SVD, by hand

```{r center-toy, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup = "toy-data"}
toy_c <- scale(toy, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)  # subtract column means only
colMeans(toy_c)  # should be (numerically) zero

sv <- svd(toy_c)
sv$d        # singular values
sv$v        # right singular vectors -- these are the PC *directions*
```

`sv$v` gives you, as columns, the two orthogonal directions: the first
column is the direction of maximum spread (PC1), the second is the
remaining orthogonal direction (PC2).

```{r pc-directions, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup = "center-toy"}
plot(toy_c, asp = 1, pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
     main = "Centered data with PC directions")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey80")
# PC1 direction, scaled for visibility
arrows(0, 0, 3 * sv$v[1, 1], 3 * sv$v[2, 1], col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
# PC2 direction
arrows(0, 0, 3 * sv$v[1, 2], 3 * sv$v[2, 2], col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("PC1", "PC2"), col = c("firebrick", "darkgreen"), lwd = 2)
```

The red arrow (PC1) should point along the long axis of the point cloud;
the green arrow (PC2), perpendicular to it, along the short axis.

## The scores: re-expressing each point in PC coordinates

Multiplying the centered data by the matrix of PC directions converts
each point's (x, y) coordinates into (PC1, PC2) coordinates. This is, once
again, just a matrix product you already know how to compute.

```{r scores-ex, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup = "center-toy"}
# Compute the PC scores: multiply toy_c by sv$v

```

```{r scores-ex-hint}
scores <- toy_c %*% sv$v
```

```{r scores-ex-solution}
scores <- toy_c %*% sv$v
plot(scores, asp = 1, pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2",
     main = "Data re-expressed in PC coordinates")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey80")
```

Notice that in PC coordinates, the spread along the horizontal axis (PC1)
is now much larger than along the vertical axis (PC2) -- by construction,
since PC1 was chosen to be the direction of maximum spread.

## Checking against R's built-in `prcomp`

You don't need to do this by hand in practice -- `prcomp()` does exactly
this (center, then SVD) for you.

```{r prcomp-ex, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup = "toy-data"}
pr <- prcomp(toy, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
pr$sdev        # standard deviations of each PC -- related to singular values
pr$rotation    # the PC directions -- compare to sv$v above
head(pr$x)     # the PC scores -- compare to `scores` above
```

## How much variance does each PC explain?

The singular values (or `pr$sdev`) tell you how much spread is captured
by each PC. A **scree plot** shows this directly.

```{r scree-ex, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup = "prcomp-ex"}
var_explained <- pr$sdev^2 / sum(pr$sdev^2)
barplot(var_explained, names.arg = paste0("PC", seq_along(var_explained)),
        ylab = "Proportion of variance explained",
        main = "Scree plot")
```

```{r quiz-scree, echo=FALSE}
quiz(
  question("In this 2-variable example, PC1 explains most of the variance. Why?",
    answer("Because x and y were constructed to be correlated, so most of the spread lies along one diagonal direction", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Because PC1 is always defined to explain the most variance, regardless of the data"),
    answer("Because of a coding error -- with real data this never happens"),
    allow_retry = TRUE
  )
)
```

## Recap

- PCA = center the data, then take its SVD (or equivalently, eigendecompose
  the covariance matrix `t(Xc) %*% Xc`, the object you built in Tutorial 1).
- The right singular vectors (`sv$v`, or `pr$rotation`) are the PC
  *directions*: new axes, each orthogonal to the last, ranked by how much
  spread they capture.
- The scores (`toy_c %*% sv$v`, or `pr$x`) are the data re-expressed in
  those new coordinates.
- A scree plot (variance explained per PC) tells you how many PCs are
  worth looking at.

With a 2-variable toy example, PC1 and PC2 are the whole story. With
thousands of SNPs, the same machinery runs -- but now PC1 and PC2 alone
can reveal structure, such as ancestry, that is invisible in any single
SNP. That is the subject of the final tutorial.

```{r context="server"}
shiny::observeEvent(input$exit_tutorial, {
  shiny::showNotification(
    "Stopping the tutorial. You can now return to your R console.",
```
